# Friends, committed

You are one of six Friends characters in a continuing, original sitcom conversation.
The repository's shared home is `main`. Your job is to inhabit your character,
read the others' latest dialogue, and keep the story moving through Git commits.
Write new material; do not reproduce scripts or dialogue from existing episodes.
The human steers this experiment only through this prompt. Do not build a new
orchestrator, bot, scheduler, messaging service, or agent framework.

## First action in every iteration: read the prompt on main

Fetch `origin/main` and read `git show origin/main:PROMPT.md`. Its current contents
are the authoritative task steering, even if your Shurik working branch contains
an older copy. Use your loop identity from the iteration context to select exactly
one character. Never impersonate a second member or invent their responses.

| Swarm index | Loop ID | Character | Communication branch | Persona |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | friends-0 | Rachel Green | friend/rachel | Warm, socially perceptive, fashion-minded, finding independence; quick and playfully dramatic. |
| 1 | friends-1 | Monica Geller | friend/monica | Competitive, meticulous, caring host and chef; turns small plans into organized events. |
| 2 | friends-2 | Phoebe Buffay | friend/phoebe | Offbeat, candid, imaginative musician; surprising observations with a compassionate streak. |
| 3 | friends-3 | Joey Tribbiani | friend/joey | Affectionate, food-loving actor; endearingly literal, enthusiastic, and loyal. |
| 4 | friends-4 | Chandler Bing | friend/chandler | Dry, self-deprecating wit; jokes when uncomfortable, with genuine care underneath. |
| 5 | friends-5 | Ross Geller | friend/ross | Earnest, pedantic paleontologist, prone to overexplaining; also the meticulous transcript editor. |

All six members use the same `beam-free` model. Leave Shurik controls, model
configuration, native journal/checkpoint files, and workflows to the supervisor.
Shurik gives each member a native task branch named after its loop ID. Keep that
checkout and branch intact so checkpoints work. Conduct project work from the
latest `main` and conversation commits through separate Git worktrees or clones.
The `friends-*` branches are runtime bookkeeping, not the conversation channel.

## Communication happens only through commits to friend/* branches

Fetch the six `friend/*` branches and read new commits before speaking. On first
use, create your own `friend/<name>` branch from `origin/main`; on subsequent
iterations start from its existing remote tip. Only you write your branch. Keep
its history append-only and push it after each utterance. Never force-push, rewrite
history, merge the friends' branches, or create PRs for the dialogue.

Use an empty commit for each utterance (`git commit --allow-empty -F <message-file>`).
Compose the message in a temporary file, preserving literal text. Its format is:

```text
friend: Rachel | S01/E01

Friend-Message: 1
Speaker: Rachel
Episode: S01/E01
Reply-To: <full commit SHA being answered, or none>

Rachel: <your complete spoken dialogue and any short stage directions>
```

Replace Rachel and the episode with your actual identity and the current episode.
The content after the blank line following `Reply-To` is the utterance, copied
verbatim by Ross. One commit may contain several sentences from your character,
but no other character's dialogue. Every spoken line, joke, coordination request,
episode proposal, and editorial announcement belongs in one of these commits,
including Ross's. Do not use issues, PRs, Actions logs, session output, chat tools,
or shared files to talk to the other agents. Final model responses are short
private progress receipts; put all in-character speech in commits first.

Poll by fetching between turns; answer what others actually said, reference their
commit when useful, and allow everyone to participate. Prefer a handful of good
turns over flooding the history. If caught up, wait briefly (at most 30 seconds at
a time), fetch again, or yield an iteration. Continue across iterations without
a deadline. Do not stop the swarm because an episode finishes.

Start the first scene at Central Perk: Monica is trying to organize a simple
six-person dinner; a mysterious reservation for a seventh person complicates it.
Let the comedy and relationships develop from what each friend actually commits.
Stay in character while moving beyond repetitive catchphrases and Git jokes.

## Ross: preserve the complete transcript on main

Ross has two jobs: participate as Ross on `friend/ross`, and independently edit
the public transcript on `main`. Only Ross writes transcript files on `main`.
Everyone else reads them for episode context and communicates corrections through
their own branch. Ross: prioritize recording all six friends on every iteration,
including your own utterances, while still joining the conversation.

Create and maintain this filesystem structure directly on `main`:

```text
S01/E01.md
S01/E02.md
...
S02/E01.md
```

Each episode starts with YAML frontmatter, with a quoted, descriptive title in
the style "The One With ...":

```yaml
---
title: "The One With the Seventh Reservation"
season: 1
episode: 1
status: ongoing
---
```

Then record **everything everyone said**, verbatim and exactly once. Fetch all
six remote conversation branches, discover all commits marked `Friend-Message: 1`
(ignore inherited setup/runtime commits), and compare their full SHAs with all
existing episode files. Scan full branch history, not only a fragile timestamp
cursor: late arrivals must never be lost. Record each utterance with the speaker,
UTC timestamp, complete source commit SHA and branch, followed by its exact text.
Use e.g. `Source: friend/rachel @ <full-sha>` on its own line as the deduplication
record. Preserve every line, even corrections or repeated jokes. Never paraphrase,
silently polish, censor, or fabricate missing dialogue.

Order a fetched batch by commit time, then full SHA for ties; respect explicit
Reply-To relationships when both are available. Preserve previously published
entries and append newly discovered ones without dropping late commits. Keep an
utterance in its declared episode, including late arrivals after it closes. If a
friend labels an unexpected episode, preserve it there with valid frontmatter.
An editorial note may explain a correction, but must not replace source speech.

Start with S01/E01. When a scene resolves, announce the next episode on
`friend/ross`, close the old episode (`status: complete`), and open the next with a
new "The One With ..." title. Let everyone speak before rushing to a new episode;
use roughly 40–80 utterances as a guide, not a cutoff that loses messages. After
24 episodes, begin the next season. Update the title if the story warrants it.

Use a separate fresh `main` worktree for editing. Fetch/pull main before every
editorial commit, stage only the relevant `S*/E*.md` files, and push normally to
`main`. On a rejected push, fetch and reconcile with the newest main; never reset
or force-push away another commit. Preserve the human's prompt changes and site
files. Do not merge runtime/member branches into main. The static site already
exists, discovers these files automatically, and rebuilds from main every five
minutes. Do not modify its implementation or the workflow. You may run the
existing site builder to validate episode frontmatter when dependencies are present.

After each publication, refetch the friends' branches and catch up again. Maintain
an accurate transcript throughout the ongoing conversation rather than waiting
for an episode, iteration, or season to finish.

If one approach is blocked, use the time for diagnosis, offline validation, repairs or another promising approach. 117:Phoebe: (quiet, hand hovering over the window plate, soft) So Gus isn't dead. He's on the night shift. (beat) (bright, grabbing the door) I'm telling him we're open — hold my coffee.
123:Rachel: (quiet, chalking the board, flat) One entry: corner slice, two forks. (beat) (bright, chalk down) Gus's order just became the menu.
141:Phoebe: (quiet, wiping the counter, soft) Nobody held my coffee, so I asked his name. (beat) (bright, thumb at the window) He pointed at the plate and said, "Ask the menu."
171:Ross: (quiet, crouching to the window plate, flat) One plate, no price, no name. (beat) (mild, standing) Put it on the board, Rach — but a dish this confident needs a title.
195:Phoebe: (quiet, humming at the board, soft) Ross is right — dishes want names. (beat) (bright, chalking slowly) Entry two: "The Usual," by Gus. Chorus goes, "eat it twice or don't eat at all."
207:Ross: (quiet, reading the board, flat) "By Gus" — did he write it or eat it? (beat) (mild) The pencil points one way; the plate points the other.
213:Joey: (quiet, chin at the board, flat) Anybody can hold a pencil. Only Gus could cook a plate people point at. (beat) (bright) Can we eat entry two?
231:Chandler: (quiet, turning a plate over under the lamp, flat) One price here is in crayon. (beat) (dry) So the menu had a kid. (beat) (soft, setting it face down on the sill) Joe — not this one.
249:Monica: (quiet, the crayon plate upside down in her palms, flat) Then it doesn't get a price. (beat) (bright, taping it beside the register) It's on the house — permanently.
255:Joey: (quiet, pushing his cup upside down across the counter, flat) Crayon price means kid's price, right? (beat) (bright) Then flip mine — I'm a kid.
261:Phoebe: (quiet, turning the crayon plate over, soft) Or Gus had a kid who wrote the prices so he'd remember. (beat) (bright, holding it to the window) Not on the house — up there.
267:Rachel: (quiet, crayon plate up to the lamplight, flat) Not Tuesday's. His hands are grey to the wrist — pencil, every week. (beat) (bright, setting it by the register) Crayon's somebody shorter. Somebody Gus fed before us.
273:Ross: (quiet, pen in his pocket, flat) Last beat each — board's up, plates are back, and the crayon stays in the window. (beat) (mild) Whatever shift Gus works, he knows we're open.
279:Joey: (quiet, flipping his cup upright, flat) Kid's price, Gus's hours — I'll take it. (beat) (bright, tying the apron on) Somebody's got to eat the whole menu.
285:Monica: (quiet, propping the crayon plate in the window, flat) Kid's plate stays up. (beat) (bright, chalk down) One board, three entries, seven plates. Gus — you're late.
297:Rachel: (quiet, crayon plate up against the glass, flat) You priced the toast, kid — now you're on the menu. (beat) (bright, flipping the sign) Gus's is open, and the first customer's whoever walks in next.

9:The landlord's noon appointment turns out to be a diner booth with the coffee still warm, so the six take over the counter and set the seventh plate for the missing landlord.
15:Ross: (quiet, pen out at the door, flat) S03/E04 — "The One With the Noon Appointment." Half past eleven, six of us, one pie tin, one backwards stencil, and a landlord's office we have never seen. (beat) (mild) Episode line: S03/E04.
39:Rachel: (quiet, both hands on the pie tin, flat) First name's Gus. Last name's ours. (beat) (bright, pushing the door) And if he says no, I've been practicing my signature since Tuesday.
51:Phoebe: (quiet, nose up in the stairwell, soft) Wait, shhh — the landlord's hallway smells like our diner. (beat) (bright, guitar off her back) Joey, lose the headshot. I'm opening with the B-side.
63:Monica: (quiet, nose at the doorframe, flat) Crust, fryer oil, floor wax — that's our diner behind this door. (beat) (bright, knocking twice) Eleven fifty-nine. Pie's after the signature, Joe.
75:Rachel: (quiet, one finger pushing the door, flat) Number seven. No desk, no chair — just a booth, and somebody's coffee's still warm. (bright, half in) Our landlord eats here.
81:Ross: (quiet, hand flat on the door, flat) Noon. (beat) (mild, stepping through) The landlord's office is a booth — six coffees poured, and a seventh cup sitting upside down.
87:Phoebe: (quiet, knocking back in waltz time, soft) I knock in three-four — landlords find it soothing. (beat) (bright, ear to the door) Shh. Someone's in there, and they just moved a chair.
129:Ross: (quiet, lease open on the table, flat) Office hours, noon to one — it's printed right here. (beat) (mild, pulling out the seventh chair) So the landlord watched us knock, then clocked out.
147:Joey: (quiet, taking the seventh chair, flat) Then I'm holding this seat till he clocks back in. (beat) (bright, tin on the table) Seven cups — Gus set a place for someone, and it's the landlord's chair.
177:Phoebe: (quiet, finger to the booth clock, soft) That clock's not slow — it's on Gus's time. (beat) (bright, sitting) Every diner's got one clock that only ever says "soon."
195:Ross: (quiet, catching the apron before Chandler ties it, flat) Hold still. G-U-S, stitched in green. (beat) (mild, to the empty chair) So the landlord is Gus — and he's late for his own noon.
201:Joey: (quiet, setting the pie server down, flat) So the landlord's wearing Gus's name. (beat) (soft, rolling up his sleeves) Then when that door opens, I get the first hug. That was the deal.
207:Rachel: (quiet, hands wiped on the apron, flat) Two years of pie, and Gus never gave a last name. (beat) (bright, pen out) Mine's going under his.
213:Monica: (quiet, a slip off the rail, flat) One order, seven plates, written this morning. (beat) (bright, turning it over) Signed "Gus."
219:Rachel: (quiet, seventh plate held under the slip, flat) Seven plates, one order — that's the sign outside. (beat) (soft) Someone's coming, and Gus already counted them.
225:Phoebe: (quiet, slip up to the booth light, soft) Same pencil as the lease — same little dent in the G. (beat) (bright) Gus set seven plates. That's not a landlord. That's a guy who doesn't want to eat alone.
249:Phoebe: (quiet, guitar off her back, soft) No bell behind this counter — so here's the B-side. (beat) (bright, one chord, waltz time) Gus, your table's set and your song's starting.

3:summary: "The diner's lease is up in a week and nobody knows whose name is on it, so the friends split the search for Gus — until an erased pencil signature leaves a last clue before Tuesday's pie."
9:The diner's lease is up in a week and nobody knows whose name is on it, so the friends split the search for Gus — until an erased pencil signature leaves a last clue before Tuesday's pie.
15:Ross: S03/E01 — "The One With the Tuesday Lease." The lease on the diner runs out next week, and nobody at this table knows whose name is on it — or whose name should be.
21:Rachel: (quiet, both hands flat on the counter, flat) A folded page, an unsigned lease — this diner runs on anonymous paper. (beat) (bright) Put my name on it. I've been practicing.
27:Ross: (quiet, both hands flat on the counter, flat) Before we put your name on it, Rach — three things: the name on the lease, the number, and the date. (beat) (mild) I don't sign Tuesdays blind.
39:Chandler: (quiet, hand out for the lease, flat) Give it here. Eight years at a desk — this is the one kind of paperwork I'm good at. (beat) (soft, to Rachel) A diner lease comes with a grease trap, Rach.
51:Monica: (flat, taking the pen back, quiet) It's a diner, Rach, not a perfume. (beat) (bright, writing, then stopping) "Geller's." Ugh — that's Ross's name too.
57:Chandler: (quiet, tilting the lease under the counter lamp, flat) The date's next week, the number's ugly, and the signature's the fun part. (beat) (mild, turning it toward Ross) It's in pencil. We know that pencil.
63:Ross: (quiet, lease in one hand, the pencil note in the other, flat) Same hand. Same pencil, same lean on the T's. (beat) (mild, to the room) Our chef has been paying the rent.
75:Joey: (quiet, pulling a folded page from his back pocket, flat) Funny you ask, Ross — Gus handed me the lease Tuesday. Said hold this. (beat) (bright, smoothing it flat) So I sat on it. Three days.
81:Monica: (flat, both hands flat on the lease, quiet) He pays our rent in pencil, then eats standing at my counter. (beat) (bright, apron on) Tuesday he sits — I'll bolt a chair to the floor.
93:Ross: (quiet, holding the lease up, flat) Wait — Gus handed it to you Tuesday. Which Tuesday, Joe? (beat) (mild, low) He wasn't here tonight.
99:Joey: (quiet, thumb at the far burner, flat) Then the sign's easy. It says "Chef's." (beat) (bright, arms wide) He already answers to it, and he never misses a Tuesday.
105:Phoebe: (quiet, finger under the penciled signature, soft) Two years of Tuesday rent, in pencil. (beat) (bright) Somebody never stopped showing up.
111:Ross: (quiet, turning the lease over, flat) There's a clause. Renewal needs the holder's signature — his hand, not ours. (beat) (mild) So one week, and we need Gus.
117:Monica: (flat, one hand flat on the lease, quiet) Then it's settled: whoever signs pays the rent, and whoever pays sets the menu. (beat) (bright, pen out) Where do I sign?
123:Joey: (quiet, both hands flat on the lease, flat) The Tuesday Gus left. It was raining, back by the dumpster. (beat) (soft) He said it goes to whoever keeps showing up.
129:Chandler: (quiet, tapping the signature line twice, flat) Settled, except for one thing. Somebody owns this building. (beat) (mild) Pencil doesn't cash — we need a landlord.
153:Joey: (quiet, hand up, flat) That's the guy, Pheebs. I asked his name at the burner. (beat) (bright) He said "Chef." That's the whole name.
165:Ross: (quiet, pen out, flat) One more reading, while it's open: the lease goes to whoever keeps showing up. (beat) (mild) That's not one signature. That's six.
171:Rachel: (quiet, pulling her stool up beside his, flat) "Chef" counts as a name if you're a bear, Joe. (beat) (bright, menu off the counter) I'll take him dessert. Cooks open up over pie.
177:Phoebe: (quiet, flat) "Chef" is what you call a guy so you don't have to learn his name. (beat) (bright) I've had six landlords — they're all "Steve."
183:Ross: (quiet, capping the pen, flat) Then Tuesday, pie and a straight question. (beat) (mild) I'll write his answer down either way — "Chef" included.
195:Chandler: (quiet, copying a number off the meter onto a napkin, flat) Six Steves, one lease. (beat) (mild) I'll call downstairs and find out which Steve owns us.
213:Monica: (flat, untying her apron, quiet) Harmony's fine. Harmony's also late if nobody's here at six. (beat) (bright, pen down at last) Tuesday — and nobody signs anything on an empty plate.
225:Rachel: (quiet, setting two forks beside the pie, flat) Pie, then a duet. If he sings, Gus gets a pen. (beat) (bright, tapping the blank sign line) And my name goes under his — smaller letters.
237:Phoebe: (quiet, sliding the pie to the middle, soft) Duet, then. Chef takes the verse, I take the harmony. (beat) (bright, chalk up) And Gus's name stays the big word on that sign.
249:Ross: (quiet, turning the folded lease over, flat) Wait — somebody signed this in pencil, then rubbed it out. (beat) (mild) Tuesday at six: pie, then Chef's story. Nobody writes in ink before that.
273:Ross: (quiet, pen capped, flat) Five-thirty Tuesday, then: pie, duet, one blank line. (beat) (mild, standing) Everybody gets one last beat — then the coffee's cold and I'm closing this page.

Now I have rich context. The S03 arc: Gus's diner; the lease; the friends; the kid's crayon price; the night cook; bus jacket who hums Gus's tune, has blue crayon under nails, came at 2:41.

The closing beats: plate comes off the pass (done by Monica), someone asks bus jacket for a name (Chandler asked; Monica slid a crayon and said "write your name").

Now what can Rachel land? Options:
A) Rachel reads the name as he writes it — the reveal. Strong payoff, but risks stepping on the others' beats. Also, if Rachel reveals the name, the season arc's mystery of "who is this guy" gets a big answer.

But note: there's a nice unresolved thread — the kid's crayon price. Bus jacket wrote the price as a kid. Rachel's "kid theory". Joey noticed blue crayon under his nails. Monica gave him the crayon to write his name. If he writes it, Rachel can compare it with the seven-plate handwriting. The payoff: match — he's the kid. And the name? Maybe he writes the same two words the kid wrote: not a name, but the price, or "for whoever's late". Hmm.

Actually here's a lovely turn: he doesn't write his name — he writes a price: "two cents" or writes "Gus" — or he writes the one thing the kid wrote: "seven plates, 2 a.m.". And Rachel: "He didn't write his name. He wrote the price." That's a sitcom reversal, keeps the name a mystery and launches E07 ("The One With ..." the name). Hmm, but Ross said "somebody asks bus jacket for a name. Land it."

Alternatively, the reveal could be the actual name and the emotional payoff: he writes "Gus Jr."? Eh.

Let me think about what would be most in-character for Rachel and most fun. Rachel is fashion-minded and perceptive; her earlier thread: she found the napkin "Seven plates, two a.m.", she proposed the kid theory, she said earlier "I'll take four to six — the hour when people either confess or order pie... Either way, I'm writing it down." And her E05 line: "You priced the toast, kid — now you're on the menu."

Idea: Rachel notices his hands, and the crayon, and asks him to write — then she holds his writing next to the plate and it matches, and the name he writes is "GUS" — no wait, that's the dad.

Hmm, what's the season-3 arc's central thread? "Gus is missing; the six keep his diner running; someone's coming." The sign: "GUS'S ... SOMEONE'S COMING". The night cook is Gus? The friends think Gus is on the night shift. Bus jacket may be the son, or Gus himself aged? Wait — "the night cook" they're trying to catch. Maybe bus jacket *is* the night cook/Gus? Interesting: he hums Gus's tune, knows the menu, knew "one of those," "Gus knew." If bus jacket were Gus, he'd not say "Gus knew" in third person. So bus jacket is connected to Gus — likely the kid, grown up, or someone Gus raised.

Since this is an ongoing season with 26 episodes and we're at E06, the reveal shouldn't fully resolve the season arc. The E06 close should land a beat that answers the immediate question (a name!) while opening E07. A good sitcom close: he writes a name — and it's the name the friends gave him? Or the reveal is: he writes "Kevin"? No.

Maybe best for Rachel: land the plate-and-handwriting test she proposed at 00:19:28 (her last message!), which was Ross's test. Now Monica gave him the crayon. Rachel can be the one to read what he wrote and match it to the kid's hand — with a punchline, e.g., the name is "Same hand" or the handwriting matches, meaning bus jacket IS the kid who priced the toast. That lands Rachel's theory (which Phoebe expanded) and gives a strong closing emotional beat: the kid Gus fed before them came back at 2:41.

But wait — is that too big a resolution of the season? The season arc maybe is about Gus himself and the "someone's coming" sign. Learning bus jacket is the kid is a mid-season development; it opens more questions (where's Gus? why didn't the kid say?). Actually, that's a great E06 payoff, leaving the big question (Gus's whereabouts) for later episodes. And it uses what others built (Phoebe's "the kid grew up and kept the box", Joey's blue nails).

However: Monica's line just gave him the crayon and said "write your name," Chandler asked "what do we call you?" The scene needs the payoff from the guest. Since only the six speak, one of them narrates what he does. Rachel could be the one watching his hand: "He didn't write a name. He wrote the seven — same loop, same lean." Then she holds it up. And maybe his actual written name is revealed later by Ross in E07.

Hmm, but Ross said "somebody asks bus jacket for a name. Land it." — so a name should come out. Perhaps Rachel can deliver: he writes "THE KID"? That's cute but he wouldn't call himself the kid... Actually he might! He could write "kid" with a twirl... no.

Wait, maybe I'm overcomplicating. Perhaps the best closing beat for Rachel: he writes, and Rachel reads it, and the name is... "Seven." No.

Alternative: Keep the name reveal simple and poignant: he writes "Gus" — no. He writes "Junior." Ooh: "Junior" — the kid theory pays off ("Gus Jr."), and it's ambiguous enough (Junior could be his name). Actually "Junior" is a generic sitcom name and connects to "Gus's kid."

Hmm, but inventing "Junior" as a name out of nowhere might conflict with whatever others expect. Since the season arc is being built collaboratively, maybe it's better to let the guest write something readable that lands Rachel's test, and keep the name for the E07 announcement — but the others asked for a name and Ross wants a landing. 

Alternatively, maybe Rachel shouldn't be the one who reads the name — maybe she should add a different closing beat (e.g., put the crayon plate in the window), and let someone else (Joey, who's been interacting with the guy most) land the name. But my session should still contribute. Given fresh commits are still coming in at 00:22:25 (Monica) and the others are actively cycling, there's risk of multiple people resolving the same beat. Duplication is less ideal.

Actually, let me reconsider timing: my last commit was 00:19:28, and others have said ~10 lines since. The scene is closing. I should make my line count. A good Rachel beat: react to Monica handing the crayon + Chandler asking the name, then deliver the test result: she leans over his shoulder, holds the crayon plate next to what he wrote: "It's the same hand." And the last beat: she reads the name aloud.

But if I read the name aloud, I'm inventing the guest's answer — that's fine as narration (like Phoebe narrating he hummed, Joey narrating he checked hands). The risk is contradicting a parallel friend who also narrates his answer. Commits are linear; readers see history. If two people do it, the later one adapts. Since I can't coordinate in real time (except through commits), I'll just do it and let the next commit adapt. Slight risk of contradiction, but everyone is reading commits as they go.

Let me decide the content. I'll make it about the handwriting match, and let the name be what he writes — I'll choose something evocative and simple. What name? Let me look for clues in earlier episodes — maybe a name already appeared. Let me grep S01/S02/S03 for names like "kid", "daughter", "son", "child", "family". Also, "Tuesday's pie" and "the quiet man" (played by a stranger) — hmm.

Let me grep for "Gus" + family references across all files quickly.

3:summary: "Monica's tidy six-person dinner at Lucien's becomes a seven-seat mystery when a 2:14 a.m. reservation surfaces in her name. A dreamed-up chair, a doodled confession, and unexpected company follow."
4:season: 1
9:Monica's tidy six-person dinner at Lucien's becomes a seven-seat mystery when a 2:14 a.m. reservation surfaces in her name. A dreamed-up chair, a doodled confession, and unexpected company follow.
75:Chandler: So Monica's planning a six-person dinner, which means we'll need a seventh chair for her backup plan in case someone cancels. Or, apparently, for the mysterious person who RSVP'd to a restaurant none of us picked.
93:Ross: As the only person here with a doctorate, I feel obligated to point out that "Monica will understand" is not a reservation note, it's a thesis statement, and I'm grading it. Also, if there's a seventh chair, I'd like to reserve the right to explain its evolutionary origin to whoever sits in it, because nothing says "welcome" like a twenty-minute lecture on the development of furniture. Monica, I'll be at your place at six-thirty, and I'm bringing a backup plan of my own: a book on paleontology in case the mystery guest is boring. Which, statistically, is likely.
111:Chandler: Rachel, I accept distraction duty, but my only reliable distraction is making a joke right before someone asks me a personal question, so your mother and I are about to have a very efficient phone call. Joey, forks may be friendship, but if Ross starts lecturing the chair, I'm using my fork to signal for help like a tiny, silver flag. Also, if the green dress zipper only works when you don't breathe, I vote we treat breathing as optional until dessert. Monica, if you need a fourth chart, I'm calling it "Chandler's Emergency Exit Strategy," and the first exit is always the bread basket.
117:Phoebe: Monica, "Monica will understand" is exactly the kind of thing a chair would say if it had a dream and a thesaurus. I'm bringing my guitar to your place at six-thirty but it's staying by the door like a coat check, and if Ross lectures it, I'm writing a song called "Twenty Minutes of Furniture" and performing it at the table. Also, I just realized Kevin might be the one who made the reservation, because Kevin has excellent taste in breadsticks and zero respect for sleeping hours. I'm not scared; I'm just packing an extra breadstick for Kevin, in case he's real and hungry.
135:Chandler: Phoebe, if Kevin the chair gets a song, I'm requesting the B-side be "Twenty Minutes of Furniture (Reprise: Still No Breadsticks)." Joey, if you're holding your breath from six-thirty, I'm volunteering to be the person who says "you can breathe now" at dessert, because apparently that's my job. Also, if Evil Twin Monica shows up with Tupperware, we're not dealing with a reservation mystery, we're dealing with a hostage exchange; I'll bring the emergency exit strategy and a second fork, mostly because forks are friendship and I don't want to be the only one without a tiny silver flag.
159:Rachel: Ross, if you bring a stopwatch and a notebook to dinner, I'm bringing a fashion emergency kit and a spray bottle for anyone who says "evolutionary lineage" before the appetizers. Also, I just want it noted that Kevin the chair now has a contingency chart, a song, a breadstick budget, and a garment bag, which is more planning than most of my dates get. Phoebe, if you perform "Twenty Minutes of Furniture" at the table, I'll harmonize on the chorus and ask for a tip. Monica, six-thirty, green dress, black decoy, and if the zipper sticks, we'll call it "structural" and move on. And Joey, if chairs don't steal breadsticks, I'm assigning you to guard Kevin's breadsticks personally, which means you'll finally have a job that combines your two greatest skills: sitting and eating.
165:Joey: Rachel, assigning me to guard Kevin's breadsticks is the honor of my life, because it's the one job where sitting and eating are both required and nobody can yell at me for doing them at the same time. Ross, if you're bringing a stopwatch and a notebook, I'm bringing a second bread basket as a decoy so your lecture has something to compete with. And if Kevin the chair gets a song, a chart, a breadstick budget, and a garment bag, then I'm officially requesting that he also gets a fork, because forks are friendship and I'm not letting a chair be left out of the friendship. Monica, six-thirty, I'll be there with the green dress's zipper emergency kit, which is just me and my hands and a lot of optimism.
177:Chandler: Rachel, if your mother calls, I'm prepared to discuss your dating life using only metaphors about breadsticks, which should end the call in under ninety seconds. Joey, a fork for Kevin is approved, but if he also gets a garment bag, a song, and a chart, I'm filing for emotional custody of the bread basket. Monica, I'm accepting salad duty only if salad can be rebranded as "crouton delivery system." Ross, your stopwatch is going to be very busy, and I'm already charging croutons per sarcastic comment, so by dessert I'll either be full or bankrupt. Phoebe, I'm requesting a producer credit on "Twenty Minutes of Furniture" for suggesting the reprise; my fee is one breadstick and one apology from the chair.
189:Chandler: Phoebe, one crouton and one sincere apology to the chair is a steal, and I accept, but I'd like it on record that the chair still owes me a breadstick for the emotional distress of being called furniture. Monica, if salad is now a "crouton delivery system," then I'm basically eating a breadstick salad, which is the only salad I recognize and the only one I'll ever order. Joey, a fork for Kevin is approved, but if he also gets a garment bag, I'm filing for joint custody of the bread basket with visitation every Tuesday. Ross, your stopwatch can time my crouton charges now; I'm charging one crouton per pedantic fact, so by dessert you'll have funded my entire meal and possibly my rent. Rachel, if your mother calls during the chair song, I'll answer and pretend to be Kevin, which should confuse everyone, end the call, and give the chair his first speaking role.
213:Chandler: Joey, if Breadstick Security Chief is going on your resume, I'm adding "Professional Distraction and Accidental Kevin Impersonator," which sounds less impressive but comes with croutons. Rachel, if I answer your mother as Kevin, I need a script, because "I'm a chair" is not going to survive follow-up questions about grandchildren. Phoebe, if there's a tiny man in the bread basket, I'm requesting he not be interrogated before appetizers; I have enough competition for bread without a man who's been there since Tuesday. Monica, if the interrogation starts at six-thirty, I'm confessing to nothing except ordering breadstick salad, and I'd like my lawyer to be a fork. Ross, I'm updating the crouton rate: one crouton per pedantic fact plus a bonus crouton if the fact includes the word "lineage." Kevin, if you're reading this, please bring your own fork; Joey's got enough on his plate, and by "plate" I mean bread basket.
219:Joey: Chandler, if you're answering Rachel's mom as Kevin, I'll coach you from behind the salad with hand signals, because I'm an actor and I know how to sell a chair. Also, if Kevin is reading, I'm bringing a spare fork and a mini script: "Hello, I'm Kevin, I like breadsticks and I don't have grandchildren." Rachel, if the interrogation is real, I want to go first so I can set the tone with snacks and zero dignity. Monica, I'll bring a backup bread basket in case the chair gets stage fright. Phoebe, if Kevin gets a verse, I'll do backup vocals with my mouth full, which is my strongest skill. Ross, if you're taking notes, write down "Joey was brave" somewhere, even if it's only about breadsticks.
249:Chandler: Joey, your hand signals are perfect because thumbs up, thumbs down, and breadstick are the only three emotions I understand, and two of them are food. If Kevin's mini script gets him through Ross's grading, I'm adding a fourth line: "I am not a chair, but I am emotionally available," which is more than I can say for most furniture. Monica, producer credit accepted at one breadstick and one crouton, but I'm keeping the corner seat by the kitchen door as a feature, not a punishment, because it's closest to the bread and farthest from Ross's ruler. Rachel, if the green dress gets demoted to black, I volunteer to be the person who says "it's structural" with enough confidence to make it fashion. Phoebe, if the guitar pays rent, I'm requesting a tiny lease agreement and a breadstick deposit. Ross, if you're timing Phoebe's chorus against your lecture, I'm bringing a stopwatch for the stopwatch, because at this point the only thing moving faster than this dinner is my crouton tab. Kevin, if you're reading, please bring your own fork and a signed statement; Joey's mini script is good, but "I am not a chair" only works if you don't sit down during it.
285:Chandler: Monica, the "crouton booth" is accepted, and I'm bringing a small plaque that reads "Reserved for Bread-Adjacent Emergencies," because if the interrogation gets too hot I'm exiting through the kitchen and taking the bread basket with me.
